title: CSCI 220: Operating Systems
text:
CSCI 220: Operating Systems
Sample University, Department of Computer Science
Term: Fall 2026

Instructor: Dr. Imaginary Person (fictional)

Course description
This course explains how an operating system manages a computer: processes, scheduling, memory, files and concurrency.

Topics
1. Processes and threads: what a process is, process states, context switching, threads vs processes.
2. CPU scheduling: first-come-first-served, shortest job first, round robin, priority scheduling.
3. Synchronization: race conditions, locks, semaphores, deadlock.
4. Memory management: paging, virtual memory, page replacement.
5. File systems: files and directories, allocation methods, journaling.
Prerequisites for this course: you should understand recursion and linked lists from CSCI 201.

Grading
Assignment 1 (Process simulator): 10%, due Friday, September 25, 2026 at 11:59 PM
Assignment 2 (Scheduler): 10%, due Friday, October 16, 2026 at 11:59 PM
Quiz 1 (processes and scheduling): 5%, in class on Wednesday, October 7, 2026
Midterm exam: 25%, Thursday, October 22, 2026, 6:00 PM to 8:00 PM
Assignment 3 (Virtual memory): 10%, due Friday, November 13, 2026 at 11:59 PM
Final exam: 40%, date set by the registrar during the December exam period

Policies
Late work loses 10% per day. The lowest quiz mark is dropped.

concepts.label: Process and process states
concepts.summary: A process is a running program; it moves through states such as ready, running and waiting.

concepts.label: Context switching
concepts.summary: The OS saves one process's state and restores another's so the CPU can be shared.

concepts.label: Threads vs processes
concepts.summary: Threads are units of execution that share a process's resources; processes are isolated from each other.

concepts.label: First-come-first-served scheduling
concepts.summary: Runs jobs in arrival order without preemption.

concepts.label: Shortest job first
concepts.summary: Runs the job with the smallest expected burst time next.

concepts.label: Round robin scheduling
concepts.summary: Gives each ready process a fixed time slice in turn.

concepts.label: Priority scheduling
concepts.summary: Runs the highest-priority ready process first.

concepts.label: Race conditions
concepts.summary: Outcomes depend on the timing of concurrent access to shared data.

concepts.label: Locks
concepts.summary: Mutual exclusion primitives that allow only one thread into a critical section at a time.

concepts.label: Semaphores
concepts.summary: Counter-based synchronization objects supporting wait and signal operations.

concepts.label: Deadlock
concepts.summary: A situation where processes wait forever for resources held by each other.

concepts.label: Paging
concepts.summary: Divides memory into fixed-size pages mapped to frames, avoiding contiguous allocation.

concepts.label: Virtual memory
concepts.summary: Gives each process an address space larger or separate from physical memory.

concepts.label: Page replacement
concepts.summary: Chooses which page to evict from memory when a new page must be loaded.

concepts.label: Files and directories
concepts.summary: Files store data; directories organize files into a hierarchy.

concepts.label: File allocation methods
concepts.summary: Strategies such as contiguous, linked or indexed allocation for placing file data on disk.

concepts.label: Journaling
concepts.summary: Logs intended changes so the file system can recover consistently after a crash.

links.label: Basic programming needed before OS concepts
Round robin uses a circular queue
Choosing shortest job is a selection by key
Page tables map pages to frames like a lookup table
Linked file allocation uses linked lists
Shared variables are what locks protect
Optimal replacement reasoning relates to lookahead
Saved state resembles stack-based call state
